findings.claim: The acceptance criteria say that if `T` carries MessagePack attributes, they are honoured. They also say contractless mode applies only when `T` has no `[DataContract]` and no `[MessagePackObject]`. Without a surrogate, `Collect` always calls `CreateContractlessMembers`, which never reads `T`'s attributes. As a result, `[MessagePackObject]` with `[Key(n)]`, `[IgnoreMember]`, `[DataContract]`, `[DataMember]` and `[IgnoreDataMember]` on `T` are all ignored. An `[IgnoreMember]` property is still serialized, and integer keys become string-keyed map entries.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.GeneratedFormatterHonoursTypeAttributesTests. HonoursIgnoreMemberOnMessagePackObjectType expects the `[IgnoreMember]` member `Secret` to be absent from the generated formatter. HonoursDataContractMembership expects the non-`[DataMember]` property `Extra` to be absent. On head both appear because contractless mode picks them up, so both tests fail.

findings.claim: This change inverts the timestamp64 range check. The requirement asks for nothing in the runtime serializer. The original check `(data64 & 0xffffffff00000000) == 0` selected the 6-byte timestamp32 form only when the upper 32 bits (nanoseconds and the high seconds bits) were zero. The new check `(data64 & 0x00000000ffffffff) == 0` selects it whenever the low 32 bits of seconds are zero, then writes only those low 32 bits. Example: `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` has seconds = 0 and nanoseconds = 100, and is written as timestamp32 value 0, so the nanoseconds are silently lost. Ordinary DateTimes now take the 10-byte timestamp64 form instead of 6 bytes, which changes the wire format.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize `new DateTime(2020,1,1,0,0,0,DateTimeKind.Utc)` and `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` with `MessagePackSerializer.Serialize` using base-built and head-built MessagePack.dll, then compare the bytes. Base gives `d6 ff ...` (6 bytes) for the first and `d7 ff ...` for the second. Head gives 10 bytes for the first and `d6 ff 00 00 00 00` for the second. Round-trip `DateTime.UnixEpoch.AddTicks(1)` on head; it deserializes as `UnixEpoch`.

findings.claim: The requirement says 'contractless behaviour over public members', and the ledger (L3) ties contractless to `ContractlessStandardResolver`. That resolver serializes public get-only members and can deserialize through a parameterized constructor. The new collector instead keeps only public read-write members. It also rejects any class without an accessible parameterless constructor by reporting MsgPack007 (lines 77-81). Immutable or record-like types from Project A therefore lose members or cannot get a formatter at all.

receipt_plan.detail: Generator test: Project A declares `public class P { public P(int id) { Id = id; } public int Id { get; } }`, and Project B declares `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class PFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<ProjectA.P>;`. On head the generator emits no formatter and reports MsgPack007, whereas `ContractlessStandardResolver` round-trips `P`.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Key control comes from a new `SurrogateType` named property on `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` (the surrogate idea from the thread). Without a surrogate, `GeneratedFormatterCollector.Collect` always uses `CreateContractlessMembers`: public read-write members, ordinal-sorted, string keys. Attributes on `T` itself are not read.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Key control comes from attributes on `T` itself (issue alternative 1 plus the maintainer's 'if there are attributes on it, we'll use them'). With a minimal edit to `Collect`, when no surrogate is given and `T` has `[MessagePackObject]` or `[DataContract]`, build members from `T`'s own `[Key]`/`[IgnoreMember]` or `[DataMember(Order/Name)]`/`[IgnoreDataMember]`. This can reuse `CreateSurrogateMembers(type, type, ...)` extended with `DataMember` support. Fall back to `CreateContractlessMembers` only when `T` has neither attribute. `SurrogateType` becomes optional or is dropped.
